thought.text: Let me isolate which command pattern triggers the podman error:

reasoning_content:
Basic commands work. The podman error came from a command that references `process-compose up` — because I was trying to kill the process-compose process, and the output of `pgrep -af "process-compose up"` is… no wait. Exit 125 with the Podman error. Something is running a podman command when I reference "process-compose".

Wait a moment, got it — is there a bash function or alias? Or… `pkill`/`kill`… no, that's not it. Actually, exit code 125 = 128-3? No, 125 is podman's exit code. The command `pgrep -af "process-compose up"` — hmm.

That's it! I got it. The terminal tool's wrapper might be running `podman exec` against some kind of "active container" context (installbench-dind-entrypoint, podman-installbench-vpn appeared in dmesg). If a command matches some kind of pattern… no wait.

Let me think: commands that failed with the podman error:
1. `curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/project/stop`
2. `kill -TERM 18011 ...; ... pgrep -af "process-compose up" ...`
3. `pgrep -af "process-compose up" | head -2; ...`

Command 1 contains "8080/project/stop" — hmm, podman error on curl to 8080? But the earlier `curl http://localhost:8080/live` worked fine!

Wait, actually maybe the process-compose process I killed (18011) was in the middle of handling `/project/stop` and… no, that's not it.

Hmm, let me look at command 2 again: it has `ps -eo pid,args --no-headers | grep -E "process-compose up|poe process-compose"`. And command 3 has `pgrep -af "process-compose up"`.

What do all three of the failed commands have in common? They contain the string "process-compose up"! And the successful `curl http://localhost:8080/live` didn't contain it. And `ps ... | grep -E "uvicorn|main.py|vite"` (no process-compose) — that was part of the failed command 2, but… command 2 was killed before reaching that point.

So it seems there's a wrapper that intercepts commands containing "process-compose up" and… no wait, the first attempt to run process-compose up also worked (nohup bash -c '... uv run poe process-compose ...' — that contained "process-compose" but not "process-compose up").

Hmm wait, in command 2: `kill -TERM 18011` killed process-compose. Then when I ran `pgrep -af "process-compose up"`…

Oh wait. Now I get it! When I killed process-compose (18011), its shutdown sequence was executed. process-compose v1.122 apparently has container integration (podman/docker), and when it shuts down, it tries to stop the containers… and that's what's producing the Podman error output! But the error came back in my terminal output with exit 125…

Hmm, actually no — the error appeared as the output of my command. `kill -TERM 18011 2>/dev/null; sleep 10; ...` — the output "Cannot connect to Podman..." appeared immediately. If the process-compose shutdown ran asynchronously, its stderr should go to its own file, not mine.

Could it be… that the terminal tool is actually running commands through some kind of container exec mechanism, and that container is now gone? dmesg mentioned "podman-installbench-vpn" and "installbench-dind-entrypoint". Maybe each terminal command runs inside an ephemeral podman container, and my kill of process-compose (18011) — no, that's not it.

Let me verify: does a command containing "process-compose up" fail? Test: `echo "process-compose up"` and `pgrep -f something_else`.
